shortDescription: By Blake BrittainTwo US senators have introduced a bill to remove a requirement that judges on the Washington, D.C.-based US Court of Federal Claims and US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit live in the D.C. area.

children: Two US senators have introduced a bill to remove a requirement that judges on the Washington, D.C.-based US Court of Federal Claims and US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit live in the D.C. area.

The bill, introduced last week and announced on Tuesday by Florida Republican Senator Ashley Moody and Delaware Democratic Senator Chris Coons, would allow judges at the courts to reside anywhere in the United States.
The Court of Federal Claims hears contract cases brought against the federal government, while the Federal Circuit most prominently hears appeals of patent cases.
Both courts have nationwide jurisdiction and currently require judges to live within 50 miles of D.C.
"For a court that covers the entire country, we should be considering nominating judges from everywhere in America based on merit — not their proximity to the D.C. bubble," Moody said in a statement.

“Americans deserve the best, most qualified judges, especially in areas like intellectual property law where expertise is key to understanding complex cases and fairly deciding the future of many entrepreneurs’ businesses,” Coons said in a statement. “For too long, we have limited the pool of judges available to take on the toughest IP and federal contract cases to those willing to uproot their lives and move to Washington, D.C.," he said.
D.C.'s other federal courts, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, do not have the same residency requirement.
The U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C. also does not have such a requirement.
